claims.text: The target materials are high-entropy alloys in an initial, unprocessed state.
High-throughput screening, multiscale modeling, and experimental validation should be applied as an integrated intervention.
Integrating high-throughput screening, multiscale modeling, and experimental validation can accelerate discovery of advanced high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach applies over a temperature range of 1000 K to 1600 K.
Solid-solution formation is a structural mediator relevant to the intervention's outcome.
Precipitation strengthening is a structural mediator relevant to the intervention's outcome.
Order-disorder transitions are structural mediators relevant to the intervention's outcome.
Combining CALPHAD-based high-throughput computation with experiments accelerates alloy discovery.
The intervention will produce high-entropy alloys with improved high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The discovered alloys will have enhanced high-temperature strength.
The discovered alloys will have enhanced ductility.
The discovered alloys will have enhanced corrosion resistance.
Arc melting, mechanical alloying, and spark plasma sintering constitute the traditional-processing baseline.
High melting temperatures limit current processing techniques for high-entropy alloys.
High hardness limits current processing techniques for high-entropy alloys.
A natural tendency to oxidize limits current processing techniques for high-entropy alloys.
Mechanical behavior of high-entropy alloys under extreme pressures and temperatures is uncertain.
Non-equilibrium interfaces in high-entropy alloys may exhibit abnormal kinetics and thermodynamics.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing microhardness, corrosion resistance, high-temperature strength, and ductility against traditionally processed alloys.
The hypothesis is falsified if traditionally processed alloys exhibit superior measured high-temperature properties.

contradictions.description: The intervention is a discovery and validation workflow, whereas the baseline and falsification experiment treat it as an alloy-processing route directly comparable to arc melting, mechanical alloying, or spark plasma sintering.
The target is defined as initially unprocessed alloys, but the proposed decisive comparison concerns alloys processed by different routes.
